propositions.text: Bills of Exchange Act mechanisms are technical but important; cheques remain popular bills of exchange in Canada.
propositions.quote: Few jurists thrive on exploring the mechanisms rooted in the Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-4 (“BEA ”); most find them technical and tedious.

propositions.text: Courts below accepted arguments disregarding BEA mechanisms, imposing undue obligations on banks.
propositions.quote: The arguments accepted by the courts below disregard those mechanisms.

propositions.text: If accepted, interpretation would require banks to determine payee liability, which lacks justification.
propositions.quote: If accepted, their interpretation would require a bank to which a third party has made a demand for payment to determine not only whether its customer is liable to pay the third party, but also whether the payee is liable to do so. No reason was advanced for imposing such an obligation.

propositions.text: Bank was not liable to pay tax debtor the cheque proceeds; appeal allowed with costs.
propositions.quote: I am of the view that the bank in this case was at no point liable to pay the tax debtor the proceeds of the cheques. I would allow the appeal with costs throughout.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds BEA mechanisms important but technical, rejects lower courts' interpretation imposing undue bank obligations, and allows the appeal with costs.

propositions.text: Section 224 ITA allows Minister to require payment owed to tax debtor to be paid to Receiver General.
propositions.quote: Section 224 of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp .) (“ITA ”), provides that the Minister of National Revenue may require a person who is, or will be within one year, liable to make a payment to a tax debtor to instead pay the money the person owes the tax debtor to the Receiver General (“requirement to pay”).

propositions.text: Minister's authority to issue requirement to pay is undisputed.
propositions.quote: The Minister’s authority to issue a requirement to pay in appropriate circumstances is not in dispute.

propositions.text: Issue is whether bank receiving cheque payable to tax debtor for deposit in joint account becomes liable to pay tax debtor.
propositions.quote: The issue in this appeal is whether a bank that receives a cheque payable to the tax debtor for deposit in an account held jointly by that debtor and a third party becomes liable to make a payment to the tax debtor.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the undisputed Minister's authority under s.224 ITA and frames the issue of bank liability on cheques payable to tax debtor for joint account deposit.

propositions.text: Facts uncontested: appellant Trustco was authorized to offer financial services in Canada and described as a bank.
propositions.quote: The facts are uncontested. At the relevant time, the appellant, Canada Trustco Mortgage Company (“Trustco”), was authorized to offer financial services in Canada. The parties have described Trustco as a bank, as has the Tax Court of Canada, and for the sake of convenience, I will also refer to it as a bank.

paragraphs.summary: The court states uncontested facts that Trustco was authorized financial services provider and described as a bank.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod was a BC lawyer with a trust account and a joint account at Trustco's Surrey branch, each governed by agreement.
propositions.quote: Cameron Clyde McLeod was a practising member of the Law Society of British Columbia. For the purposes of his law practice, he maintained a trust account with Trustco at the latter’s King George Highway branch in Surrey, B.C. In addition, he and another lawyer, Herbert Maier, held a joint account at the same branch. Each of the accounts was governed by an agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. McLeod held a trust account and a joint account at Trustco's Surrey branch, each governed by agreement.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod owed federal tax; Minister issued three requirements to pay to Trustco to pay Receiver General instead of McLeod.
propositions.quote: Mr. McLeod owed tax to the federal government. The Minister became aware that cheques payable to Mr. McLeod were being drawn on the trust account and deposited in the joint account. The Minister issued three requirements to pay to Trustco. According to these requirements, Trustco was to pay to the Receiver General moneys otherwise payable to Mr. McLeod.

propositions.text: Trustco disputed liability, arguing it was not indebted to taxpayer alone.
propositions.quote: In response to the requirements to pay, Trustco disputed its liability on the ground that it was “not indebted to the [taxpayer] alone”.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. McLeod owed tax; Minister issued requirements to pay to Trustco; Trustco disputed liability as not indebted to taxpayer alone.

propositions.text: Cheques were issued during requirements' effectiveness, drawn on trust account, payable to McLeod, delivered with deposit instructions to joint account.
propositions.quote: Each of the cheques on which the claim is based was issued during the period of effectiveness of the requirements to pay, was drawn on the trust account, was payable to Mr. McLeod and was delivered to Trustco with an instruction to deposit the funds in the joint account.

propositions.text: Instruction was written on back of cheque; identity and authority of deliverer not in issue; Trustco credited joint account, sent cheques for processing, debited trust account next day.
propositions.quote: This instruction was given by writing “Dep to” and the account number on the back of the cheque. Although the evidence is silent as to the identity of the person or persons who delivered the cheques and gave the instructions to deposit them, neither the authority to do so of the person or persons in question nor the legitimacy of Trustco’s receipt of the cheques for deposit is at issue. Trustco credited the joint account, sent the cheques to a third party for collection, processing and settlement — the third party’s stamp appears on the back of the cheque filed as a sample — and, on the following day, debited the trust account.

paragraphs.summary: The court states cheques were drawn on trust account payable to McLeod, delivered with deposit instructions to joint account; Trustco processed accordingly.

propositions.text: Minister assessed Trustco for failing to comply with requirements; Trustco objected and appealed to Tax Court after rejection.
propositions.quote: The Minister assessed Trustco for the amounts of the cheques for failing to comply with the three requirements to pay. Trustco filed notices of objection. After they were rejected, it appealed to the Tax Court of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Minister assessed Trustco; Trustco objected and appealed to Tax Court after rejection.

propositions.text: Bank-customer relationship is contractual with implied and express terms; cheque transactions involve bank as drawee, negotiating or collecting bank; customer as drawer or holder.
propositions.quote: A bank’s relationship with a customer is based on a contract made up of both implied and express terms; I will elaborate on this below. Where a cheque is involved, the parties’ rights and obligations are also governed by the BEA . In most transactions involving cheques, a bank acts in only one capacity, that is, as either the drawee, the negotiating bank or the collecting bank, and the bank’s customer acts as either the drawer or the holder of a cheque.

propositions.text: In this case, Trustco acted as collecting bank and drawee; McLeod acted as drawer, payee, and joint account holder.
propositions.quote: In this case, Trustco acted at times as the collecting bank and at other times as the drawee. Mr. McLeod acted variously as the drawer (he was the holder of the trust account), as the payee of the cheques (the cheques were made out to him) and as one of the two holders of the joint account.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains bank-customer contractual relationship and roles; here Trustco acted as collecting bank and drawee; McLeod as drawer, payee, and joint account holder.

propositions.text: Canada conceded requirements to pay do not apply to funds in trust or joint accounts; Trustco had no obligation to remit those funds.
propositions.quote: It is also important to point out that the respondent, Her Majesty The Queen (hereinafter referred to as “Canada”) made two significant concessions at trial (2008 TCC 482, [2009] 1 C.T.C. 2264, at para. 11): (a) the requirements to pay do not apply to funds on deposit in the trust account, and Trustco accordingly had no obligation to remit funds on deposit in the trust account; and (b) the requirements to pay do not apply to funds in the joint account, and Trustco accordingly had no obligation to remit funds on deposit in the joint account.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Canada conceded requirements to pay do not apply to funds in trust or joint accounts; Trustco had no obligation to remit those funds.

propositions.text: Question is whether Trustco was liable to pay McLeod because he was named payee of cheques, not because of funds in accounts.
propositions.quote: Since Canada’s position does not rest on funds being held in the trust account or in the joint account, the question becomes whether Trustco was liable to make payments to the tax debtor, Mr. McLeod, because of the fact that he was named as the payee of the cheques.

propositions.text: Trustco's obligations must be examined in two capacities: as collecting bank and as drawee of the cheque.
propositions.quote: To answer this question, Trustco’s obligations must be examined in the two capacities in which it acted, as mentioned above: (1) as the collecting bank and (2) as the drawee of the cheque.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue as Trustco's liability due to McLeod as payee, requiring examination of Trustco's obligations as collecting bank and drawee.

propositions.text: Little J. dismissed Trustco’s appeal applying National Trust Co. test on s.224(1) ITA, focusing on repayment of trust account funds.
propositions.quote: Little J. dismissed Trustco’s appeal. He applied the test from National Trust Co. v. Canada (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 704 (F.C.A.), to determine whether s. 224(1) of the ITA had been triggered. He asked whether Trustco was “liable” to make a payment and whether the amount would be “payable” to a tax debtor within a year. The need to “stop [the analysis] before considering that it was cheques that were presented to the bank” was pivotal to his reasoning (para. 20). He focussed on the “repayment” of the funds in the trust account (para. 12 (emphasis in original)).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Little J. dismissed Trustco’s appeal applying National Trust Co. test, focusing on repayment of trust account funds.

propositions.text: Little J. found proceeds payable to McLeod due to debtor-creditor relationship requiring repayment on demand.
propositions.quote: Little J. considered that the proceeds of the cheques were “payable” to Mr. McLeod because the debtor-creditor relationship between Trustco and Mr. McLeod required the former to repay the funds deposited in the trust account to the account holder on demand (para. 22).

propositions.text: Liability arose when McLeod presented cheques to bank; no need to examine transfer from trust to joint account.
propositions.quote: In his view, Trustco’s liability arose when Mr. McLeod “presented the bank with the cheques” (para. 28). This led Little J. to conclude that he did not need to examine the fact that the moneys had actually been transferred from the trust account to the joint account (para. 30).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Little J. found proceeds payable to McLeod due to debtor-creditor relationship and liability arose on cheque presentment, ignoring transfer to joint account.

propositions.text: Little J. found cheque writing not withdrawal, but presentment changed situation; McLeod as drawer could enforce payment.
propositions.quote: In addition, although he acknowledged that the “writing [of] a cheque is not by itself a withdrawal”, Little J. found that the situation was different once “the cheque is presented to the bank” (para. 31). He took into consideration the fact that Mr. McLeod was not only the payee but also the drawer and that as the drawer he was in a position to enforce the payment because of the debtor-creditor relationship that existed between Trustco and himself (ibid.).

propositions.text: Little J. recognized bank not liable to payee but liable to McLeod as trust account holder; accepted Canada’s submission McLeod was cheque bearer.
propositions.quote: Little J. recognized — and he noted that Canada had conceded the point — that a bank is not liable to the payee of a cheque (para. 39). However, in his view, Trustco remained liable to pay the cheques to Mr. McLeod in his capacity as holder of the trust account. He accepted Canada’s submission that Mr. McLeod was the bearer of the cheque (para. 41).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Little J. found cheque presentment changed liability; bank liable to McLeod as trust account holder, not payee; McLeod was cheque bearer.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal upheld Little J.’s decision unanimously, finding no palpable or overriding error.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal found that no “palpable or overriding error” had been made and unanimously upheld Little J.’s decision (2009 FCA 267, 2009 DTC 5171 (p. 6205), at para. 1).

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Federal Court of Appeal unanimously upheld Little J.’s decision without palpable or overriding error.

propositions.text: Trustco argues trial judge failed to distinguish demand for repayment and cheque delivery for deposit; liable only as drawee on proper presentment.
propositions.quote: Trustco argues that the trial judge failed to differentiate between a demand for repayment of funds deposited in an account and the delivery of a cheque for deposit. In its view, it was liable only — as drawee — to pay funds out of the trust account upon proper presentment for payment by the holder of the cheque. At no point was it liable to make a payment to Mr. McLeod, the tax debtor.

paragraphs.summary: Trustco argues trial judge erred by conflating repayment demand and cheque deposit; liable only as drawee on proper presentment, not to McLeod.

propositions.text: Canada contends no distinction between cheque presentment for cash payment and for deposit; McLeod's depositor role irrelevant.
propositions.quote: Canada contends that there is no distinction between presentment of a cheque to the drawee for the payment of cash to Mr. McLeod and presentment of a cheque for deposit to the joint account. Its position is that when Mr. McLeod delivered the cheques to Trustco and instructed it to pay the amounts into the joint account, he acted as payee, creditor, drawer and depositor, but that his role as depositor is irrelevant.

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues no distinction between cheque presentment for cash or deposit; McLeod's depositor role is irrelevant.

propositions.text: Canada's contention implies Trustco became liable on cheque acceptance for deposit; requires review of legal relationships.
propositions.quote: Canada’s contention implies that Trustco became liable to make a payment to Mr. McLeod when it accepted the cheque for deposit. To determine whether Trustco is liable to make a payment to the Receiver General, it will be necessary to review the relevant legal relationships.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Canada's contention implies Trustco became liable on cheque acceptance; legal relationships must be reviewed.

propositions.text: Foley v. Hill establishes banker-customer relationship as debtor-creditor, with bank obligated to repay on demand.
propositions.quote: The relation between a Banker and Customer, who pays money into the Bank, is the ordinary relation of debtor and creditor . . . . . . . . . . I am now speaking of the common position of a banker, which consists of the common case of receiving money from his customer on condition of paying it back when asked for, or when drawn upon, or of receiving money from other parties, to the credit of the customer, upon like conditions to be drawn out by the customer, or, in common parlance, the money being repaid when asked for, because the party who receives the money has the use of it as his own, and in the using of which his trade consists, and but for which no banker could exist, especially a banker who pays interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Foley v. Hill establishing banker-customer debtor-creditor relationship with repayment obligation on demand.

propositions.text: Debtor-creditor relationship implies bank must repay funds on customer demand; Trustco has separate contracts for trust and joint accounts.
propositions.quote: Implicit in the debtor-creditor relationship is the bank’s obligation to repay the funds deposited in the account when its customer demands payment. In the case at bar, Trustco is a party in two separate contractual relationships: the first is in connection with the trust account and the second with the joint account.

propositions.text: Canada conceded it cannot attach funds in trust or joint accounts; focuses on cheques payable to McLeod, narrowing issues.
propositions.quote: Having conceded that it cannot attach funds in either of these accounts, Canada cannot rely merely on the debtor-creditor relationships that arose from the fact that funds were at some point in time held in them. Canada accordingly focusses on the fact that cheques were made to the order of Mr. McLeod, the tax debtor, which narrows the issues and makes it necessary to review the obligations a bank must meet upon receipt of a cheque for deposit and upon presentment of a cheque drawn on it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds debtor-creditor relationship implies repayment obligation; Canada conceded no attachment of funds; focuses on cheques payable to McLeod.

propositions.text: Canada argues cheque receipt for deposit involves two steps: demand as payee and drawer, then instruction to deposit to joint account.
propositions.quote: Counsel for Canada argues that the best way to view the receipt of the cheques for deposit is to break the transactions down into two steps: at the first, Mr. McLeod demanded to be paid as payee of the cheques and also demanded, as drawer, that the amounts be repaid out of funds owed to him in relation to the trust account; at the second, he instructed Trustco to deposit the funds into the joint account.

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues cheque receipt for deposit involves demand as payee and drawer, then instruction to deposit to joint account.

propositions.text: Cheques were received with instructions to deposit into joint account, not to pay Mr. McLeod as payee.
propositions.quote: The evidence shows that the cheques were initially received at the branch with instructions to deposit the funds into the joint account, not that Mr. McLeod, as drawer, demanded that payments be made to him as payee.

propositions.text: Cheques credited to joint account before clearing and debit from trust account; Trustco never paid Mr. McLeod directly.
propositions.quote: The evidence is also clear that the cheques were credited to the joint account before being sent for clearing and before the funds were debited from the trust account. At no point did Trustco actually make a payment to Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds cheques were deposited into joint account per instructions; Trustco never paid Mr. McLeod directly.

propositions.text: Cheque is an instrument embodying common law and statutory concepts, governed by BEA and common law.
propositions.quote: A cheque is an instrument that embodies both common law and statutory concepts. This means that both the statute governing the instrument — the BEA — and the common law must be taken into consideration.

paragraphs.summary: Court states cheque involves both BEA statute and common law concepts.

propositions.text: Tax Court judge's finding that Mr. McLeod was bearer is inconsistent with BEA definition of bearer.
propositions.quote: The argument accepted by the Tax Court judge that Mr. McLeod was the bearer of the cheque (para. 41) is inconsistent with the definition of the term “bearer” in the BEA

propositions.text: Bearer is person in possession of bill payable to bearer; cheque must be payable to bearer or endorsed in blank to be bearer.
propositions.quote: a bearer is a specific type of holder, namely “the person in possession of a bill or note that is payable to bearer” (s. 2 BEA ). To be payable to bearer, a cheque must be expressed to be so payable, or the only or last endorsement on it must be an endorsement in blank (s. 20(3) BEA ).

propositions.text: Cheques here were not payable to bearer nor endorsed in blank; Mr. McLeod was not in possession or holder after deposit.
propositions.quote: In this case, the cheques were neither expressed to be payable to bearer nor endorsed in blank. After the cheques had been delivered for deposit into the joint account, Mr. McLeod was no longer in possession of them, was not entitled to them and was therefore not their holder.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Tax Court judge erred; Mr. McLeod was not bearer or holder after deposit as cheques not payable to bearer or endorsed in blank.

propositions.text: Canada's and Tax Court's approach disregards Trustco's capacity as collecting bank with obligations under common law and banking agreement.
propositions.quote: More importantly, Canada’s approach and the Tax Court judge’s interpretation disregard the capacity in which Trustco acted.

propositions.text: Bank receiving cheque for deposit acts as collecting bank with duty to present cheque for payment and collect proceeds.
propositions.quote: When a customer, the payee of a cheque, deposits a cheque or other instrument in an account with the customer’s bank, that bank takes on the role of collecting bank, which involves presenting the cheque for payment through the clearing system to the paying bank

propositions.text: Bank has implied contractual duty to honour cheques and collect proceeds for customer's account.
propositions.quote: the duty to collect the proceeds of a cheque was characterized as one of the common law incidents of the banking contract: “The bank undertakes to receive money and to collect bills for its customer’s account”

propositions.text: If customer silent, bank presumed to act as collecting bank.
propositions.quote: when the customer is silent about what is expected from the bank, the bank may be presumed to act as a collecting bank

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Canada and Tax Court ignore Trustco's role as collecting bank with duties under common law and contract to collect cheque proceeds.

propositions.text: Collecting bank's duty requires properly payable cheque and no suspicious circumstances; bank must act with reasonable care and notify dishonour if applicable.
propositions.quote: For the collecting bank’s duty to its customer to be triggered, there must be a properly payable cheque and no suspicious circumstances. In undertaking to collect a deposited cheque, the collecting bank must select the collection method with reasonable care, promptly present the deposited cheque for collection, receive payment for it and credit the customer’s account or, if applicable, give notice of dishonour

paragraphs.summary: Court states collecting bank's duty requires proper cheque, no suspicion, reasonable care, prompt presentment, payment receipt, and notice of dishonour.

propositions.text: Bank crediting account before receiving proceeds raises conceptual issue but is practically unimportant in Canada due to s.165(3) BEA.
propositions.quote: The situation of a bank that credits its customer’s account before actually receiving the proceeds of collection raises, in Crawford’s words (p. 24-6), an “interesting conceptual problem”. However, as he correctly points out, this interesting question is of no practical importance in Canada.

propositions.text: Section 165(3) BEA gives bank receiving cheque for deposit rights and powers of holder in due course.
propositions.quote: Section 165(3) of the BEA provides that a bank which receives a cheque for deposit acquires all the rights and powers of a holder in due course

paragraphs.summary: Court notes conceptual issue of crediting before proceeds received but s.165(3) BEA grants bank holder in due course rights, making issue practically unimportant.

propositions.text: Trustco received cheques from payee or agent with instructions to deposit to joint account; contract authorized accepting cheques with account number.
propositions.quote: Trustco was put in possession of the cheques by the payee, Mr. McLeod, or by someone acting on his behalf, with instructions to deposit them. Not only was Mr. McLeod one of the holders of the joint account, but Trustco’s contract with the account’s holders authorized it to accept cheques from persons who provided the account number.

propositions.text: No suggestion instructions were invalid; Trustco lawfully possessed cheques and acquired rights of holder in due course under s.165(3) BEA.
propositions.quote: Since Trustco was in lawful possession of the cheques, it can safely be concluded that, once it had received the cheques for deposit and credited them to the joint account, it acquired the rights of a holder in due course pursuant to s. 165(3) of the BEA

propositions.text: Trustco had contractual obligation to joint account holders to present cheques for payment.
propositions.quote: and was under a contractual obligation to the holders of the joint account to present the cheques for payment.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Trustco lawfully possessed cheques, acquired holder in due course rights, and owed contractual duty to joint account holders to present cheques.

propositions.text: Presentment is precondition for payment; must be made by holder and payment made to holder under BEA.
propositions.quote: With some exceptions that do not apply in this case, presentment is a precondition for payment (s. 84(1) BEA ). Presentment must be made by a holder (s. 84(3) BEA ), and payment must be made to a holder (s. 138(2) BEA ).

propositions.text: Cheque processing is based on banks' contractual duty to collect for account holders; Trustco collected for joint account holders, not Mr. McLeod alone.
propositions.quote: The manner in which cheques deposited into bank accounts are processed is grounded in the premise that banks deal primarily with persons who hold accounts with them and in the implicit contractual undertaking of banks to collect the proceeds of cheques deposited in their customers’ accounts. In this case, Trustco collected the cheques on behalf of Mr. McLeod and Mr. Maier jointly, not of Mr. McLeod alone.

propositions.text: Good reasons exist not to confound joint account holders with a single holder.
propositions.quote: As the Chief Justice acknowledges, there are good reasons not to confound the holders of a joint account with a single one of its holders

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod as payee cannot be confused with joint account holders even though he is one of them.
propositions.quote: This means that in the instant case, the payee, Mr. McLeod, cannot be confused with the holders of the joint account even though he is one of them.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains presentment/payment rules and finds Trustco collected for joint account holders, not Mr. McLeod alone, who cannot be conflated with joint holders.

propositions.text: Contract clauses allow Trustco to accept deposits and debit joint account if cheque returned unpaid.
propositions.quote: there was a clause to the effect that the amount of any instrument previously cashed, negotiated or credited by Trustco and returned unpaid or unsettled could be debited from the joint account.

propositions.text: Clauses relevant to bank crediting account then presenting cheque; do not imply Trustco liable to pay Mr. McLeod on receipt alone.
propositions.quote: These clauses are relevant to a situation in which a bank receives a cheque, credits an account and then presents the cheque for payment. If the cheque is returned unpaid, the collecting bank may debit its customer’s account. The clauses in question do not support an inference that the receipt of a cheque for deposit in the joint account would on its own suffice for Trustco to become liable to make a payment to Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds contract clauses allow Trustco to accept deposits and debit account if unpaid, but do not make Trustco liable to pay Mr. McLeod on receipt alone.

propositions.text: Trustco had to be alert to suspicious circumstances but trust account status is not material to bank duties.
propositions.quote: Trustco had to be alert to suspicious circumstances. However, the fact that cheques are drawn on a trust account is not material to the collecting bank’s duties.

propositions.text: Generally, banks are not required to police trust accounts.
propositions.quote: it is generally not incumbent on a bank to police a trust account

propositions.text: Trustco acted on contract with joint account holders, not as agent for Mr. McLeod alone; debiting trust account was not payment to Mr. McLeod alone.
propositions.quote: In crediting the joint account, sending the cheques to a third party for clearing, and receiving the proceeds, Trustco was acting on the basis of its contractual relationship with the holders of the joint account and not on behalf of Mr. McLeod personally. When Trustco debited the trust account the next day, it was not making a payment to Mr. McLeod or to an agent acting for him alone.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Trustco acted under contract with joint account holders, not Mr. McLeod alone, and trust account status does not affect bank duties.

propositions.text: Chief Justice's opinion that Trustco never became holder is incorrect; s.165(3) BEA grants holder in due course rights despite lack of endorsement.
propositions.quote: With respect, the fact that the cheques were not endorsed does not mean that Trustco did not acquire the rights of a holder in due course which results from having received valid cheques in good faith. Section 165(3) of the BEA was in fact adopted to avoid the argument that a bank that receives for deposit a cheque bearing a restrictive endorsement or no endorsement at all is not a holder

propositions.text: Section 165(3) BEA prevents argument that bank receiving cheque without endorsement is not holder; purpose not to protect against fraudulent endorsements.
propositions.quote: Section 165(3) of the BEA was in fact adopted to avoid the argument that a bank that receives for deposit a cheque bearing a restrictive endorsement or no endorsement at all is not a holder — its purpose was not to protect against fraudulent endorsements

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting s.165(3) BEA interpretation.
propositions.quote: see s. 67(2) BEA ; Boma Manufacturing Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, [1996] 3 S.C.R. 727, at paras. 76-81; J.C. Creations Ltd. v. Vancouver City Savings Credit Union, 2004 BCCA 107, 236 D.L.R. (4th) 602; Westboro Flooring & Décor Inc. v. Bank of Nova Scotia (2004), 241 D.L.R. (4th) 257 (Ont. C.A.)

propositions.text: Trustco's holder in due course status not reason for no liability; reason is acting as collecting bank for joint account holders, not as agent for Mr. McLeod alone.
propositions.quote: The reason Trustco owed no money to Mr. McLeod is that it was acting as the collecting bank for its customers, the holders of the joint account. It did not collect the proceeds of the cheques as agent for the payee, Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Chief Justice's view; Trustco was holder in due course but owed no money to Mr. McLeod as it acted for joint account holders, not as his agent.

propositions.text: Chief Justice relies on B.M.P. case where collecting bank acted as agent for payee, but facts differ here as payee and account holder were same in B.M.P.
propositions.quote: The Chief Justice relies on B.M.P. Global Distribution Inc. v. Bank of Nova Scotia... In that case, because the payee had instructed its bank to deposit the cheque into its own account, the distinction in the instant case between the payee and the account holder on whose behalf the cheque is collected did not arise.

propositions.text: In B.M.P., bank acted as agent for person whose account cheque was deposited into; wording should be precise to that effect.
propositions.quote: Since the contractual duty to collect the proceeds of a cheque is owed to the customer in whose account the cheque is deposited, it would have been more precise to say that the collecting bank acts as agent for the person in whose account the cheque has been deposited.

propositions.text: B.M.P. wording on agency cannot support holding that collecting bank has contract with payee other than account holder.
propositions.quote: This choice of words in a case dealing with mistake of fact and tracing cannot serve as a basis for holding that a collecting bank has a contractual relationship with someone other than the holder of the account to which the cheque is credited.

paragraphs.summary: Court distinguishes B.M.P. case, noting collecting bank acts as agent for account holder, not payee if different; B.M.P. wording not basis for contrary holding.

propositions.text: Only instructions were to deposit cheques to joint account, triggering duty to collect proceeds owed to joint account holders.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the only instructions received were to deposit the cheques to the credit of the joint account, and it is these instructions that triggered the duty to collect the proceeds of the cheques.

propositions.text: Contract imposing duty to collect is between Trustco and joint account holders; no contract between bank and payee as payee.
propositions.quote: The contract that incorporates the implied term imposing on the bank the duty to proceed to collect on the cheque is the one between Trustco and the holders of the joint account. There is no contract between a bank and a payee in his or her capacity as payee.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds duty to collect arises from contract with joint account holders, not with payee as payee.

propositions.text: Approach is not formalistic; cheque clearing process does not create liability to pay Receiver General; obligation is to joint account holders.
propositions.quote: This approach is not formalistic. No significance is attached to the fact that the cheques were processed through the clearing system. Trustco’s acceptance of the cheques for deposit in the joint account could not have resulted in a liability to pay the Receiver General: the obligation resulting from that acceptance was to the holders of the joint account

propositions.text: Canada concedes funds in joint account could not be attached.
propositions.quote: Canada concedes that the funds in the joint account could not be attached.

paragraphs.summary: Court states approach is not formalistic; Trustco's obligation is to joint account holders; Canada concedes funds in joint account not attachable.

propositions.text: Canada argues focus should be on Mr. McLeod as payee and creditor demanding payment from Trustco as drawee.
propositions.quote: Canada nonetheless contends that the focus should be on the fact that Mr. McLeod was acting in this case in his capacity as payee and as a creditor of Trustco by virtue of his status as holder of the trust account, and that he was demanding payment from Trustco in its capacity as drawee.

propositions.text: Chief Justice accepts this argument; court will explain why it must fail.
propositions.quote: Since the Chief Justice accepts this argument, I will now explain why it must fail.

paragraphs.summary: Canada argues Mr. McLeod as payee demands payment from Trustco; Chief Justice accepts; court will explain why argument fails.

propositions.text: Schroeder case holds cheque is request to pay, not assignment; drawee bank owes no liability to payee absent statute.
propositions.quote: A cheque is a request to pay and nothing more; it does not purport to be an assignment, and it is impossible, therefore, to regard it as an assignment of so much money. The bankers hold their customer’s money on an implied contract to pay his cheques up to the amount of his balance in their hands, for breach of which they would be liable in damages to the drawer. But there is no contract by the bankers with the payees of the cheque, and they can have no remedy against the bank unless by the statute.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Schroeder: cheque is request to pay; drawee bank owes no liability to payee absent statute.

propositions.text: Foley v. Hill reasoning consistent: banker's obligation arises from debtor-creditor relationship with customer, not payee.
propositions.quote: This approach is consistent with the reasoning in Foley v. Hill. A banker’s obligation arises out of the debtor-creditor relationship created when a bank account is opened. The payee is not a party to this contractual relationship, and the mere fact of being a payee does not entail such a relationship with the drawee.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Foley v. Hill supports that bank's obligation is to customer, not payee, who has no contract with drawee.

propositions.text: BEA defines cheque as bill drawn on bank payable on demand; bill is unconditional order to pay sum certain to specified person or bearer.
propositions.quote: For the purpose of determining whether, absent any contractual relationship with the payee of a cheque, a drawee bank owes the payee any duty, the definition of a cheque in the BEA is relevant: “A cheque is a bill drawn on a bank, payable on demand” (s. 165(1) ). A bill is defined as follows (s. 16(1) BEA ): 16. (1) A bill of exchange is an unconditional order in writing, addressed by one person to another, signed by the person giving it, requiring the person to whom it is addressed to pay, on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time, a sum certain in money to or to the order of a specified person or to bearer.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites BEA definition of cheque as bill drawn on bank payable on demand to specified person or bearer.

propositions.text: BEA s.126 states cheque issuance does not assign funds in drawee's hands; drawee not liable if does not accept.
propositions.quote: In addition, the BEA explicitly states that the mere issuance of a cheque does not operate as an assignment of funds in the hands of the drawee (s. 126 BEA ): 126. A bill, of itself, does not operate as an assignment of funds in the hands of the drawee available for the payment thereof, and the drawee of a bill who does not accept as required by this Act is not liable on the instrument.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites BEA s.126: cheque issuance does not assign funds; drawee not liable if does not accept.

propositions.text: Provisions mirror Schroeder principles: cheque is order to pay from customer's account; no drawee obligation to payee absent contract or statute.
propositions.quote: These provisions, read together, mirror the principles stated in Schroeder and incorporate them into the statute. A cheque operates neither as an assignment of funds in the hands of the payee nor as an assignment of funds in the hands of the drawee. It is a document by means of which a customer orders his or her banker to pay funds the banker owes the customer to a person or to the order of that person out of the account specified on it. In and of itself, a cheque imposes no obligation on a drawee bank to the payee.

propositions.text: Canada accepted this interpretation at trial.
propositions.quote: This interpretation is well entrenched in our law and was accepted by Canada at trial

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting no drawee obligation to payee absent contract or statute.
propositions.quote: Schroeder; Thomson v. Merchants Bank of Canada (1919), 58 S.C.R. 287, at p. 298; Schimnowski Estate, Re, [1996] 6 W.W.R. 194 (Man. C.A.), at para. 19.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds BEA and case law confirm no drawee obligation to payee absent contract or statute; Canada accepted this at trial.

propositions.text: The statutory duty of a bank to pay a cheque is governed by presentment rules, which are generally mandatory under s. 84(1) BEA.
propositions.quote: The statutory duty of a bank to pay a cheque is governed by the rules applicable to presentment. With some exceptions, as I mentioned above, presentment is mandatory (s. 84(1) BEA ).

propositions.text: General rule for presentment: must be made by holder or authorized person at proper place to designated payer or authorized representative if found with reasonable diligence (s. 86(1) BEA).
propositions.quote: The general rule for presentment of a cheque is as follows (s. 86(1) BEA ): 86. (1) Presentment of a bill must be made by the holder or by a person authorized to receive payment on his behalf, at the proper place as defined in section 87, and either to the person designated by the bill as payer or to his representative or a person authorized to pay or to refuse payment on his behalf, if with the exercise of reasonable diligence such person can there be found.

propositions.text: Bank may incur other liabilities upon acceptance under s. 34 BEA, but that is not the case here as Mr. McLeod was no longer a holder at presentment; only Trustco had holder rights.
propositions.quote: A bank may incur other liabilities in circumstances which do not arise in the case at bar, upon acceptance within the meaning of s. 34 of the BEA , for example. That is not the case here. At the time of presentment, Mr. McLeod was no longer a holder. Only Trustco had the rights and powers of a holder in due course.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the statutory duty of banks to pay cheques is governed by mandatory presentment rules under the BEA, and only Trustco had holder rights at presentment.

propositions.text: The duty to honour a cheque is triggered only when the holder presents it to the drawee for payment, as illustrated by Bank of Montreal case.
propositions.quote: Bank of Montreal illustrates clearly that the duty to honour the customer’s cheque is triggered only at the time the holder presents the cheque to the drawee for payment.

propositions.text: In Bank of Montreal, the tax debtor was no longer bearer at presentment after endorsement by his wife, so not entitled to proceeds at that time.
propositions.quote: Garon T.C.C.J. found, correctly in my view, that [i]n the present case the moneys payable by virtue of the two cheques in issue were not payable to the tax debtor, since at the time of presentment of the cheques to the bank, after the endorsement by Mrs. Lynn Morgan, Mr. Morgan was no longer the bearer of these cheques.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the duty to honour a cheque arises only at presentment by the holder, citing Bank of Montreal where the debtor was not bearer at presentment.

propositions.text: Capital Associates case confirms that depositing a cheque is not presentment for payment; only presentment triggers bank's duty to pay.
propositions.quote: Capital Associates Ltd. v. Royal Bank of Canada ... Capital, in depositing the cheque, did not demand payment, but gave authority to the bank to present the cheque for payment to All-Canadian.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal distinguished deposit from presentment, holding bank not responsible when payment was stopped before presentment.
propositions.quote: All-Canadian refused to pay, and the bank cannot be responsible to Capital.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Capital Associates held deposit is not presentment, so bank owes no duty to pay if payment is stopped before presentment.

propositions.text: Distinction between deposit and presentment is critical; bank owes no duty to pay until cheque is presented for payment.
propositions.quote: Capital Associates illustrates not only the distinction between delivery of a cheque for deposit and presentment for payment, but also the rationale for the rules that a bank to which a payee delivers a cheque owes no duty to that person as payee and that it is only when the cheque is presented to the bank in its capacity as drawee that it is requested to disburse the funds.

propositions.text: Many intervening circumstances can occur between cheque issuance and presentment, including stop payment, negotiation, delay, insolvency.
propositions.quote: Between the time the cheque is issued and the time it is presented for payment, many intervening circumstances are possible: for example, payment could be stopped as in Capital Associates, the cheque could be negotiated to a third party, an excessive delay could occur, or the drawer could become insolvent or incapacitated.

propositions.text: Bank does not assume risks between deposit and presentment; funds used to pay cheque belong to drawer who promises payment upon presentment (s. 129 BEA).
propositions.quote: In general, a bank does not assume any risks that may be incurred between the time it receives the cheque for deposit and the time it presents the cheque to the drawee for payment. The funds used by the drawee bank to pay the cheque are funds of the drawer. ... it is the drawer who promises that upon presentment, payment will be made (s. 129 BEA ).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains deposit differs from presentment; bank owes no duty until presentment, and the drawer promises payment upon presentment under s.129 BEA.

propositions.text: Drawee bank's obligation to pay is to the drawer and triggered only upon presentment by the holder or agent (except as provided in BEA).
propositions.quote: It is clear from the rules applicable to presentment that the drawee bank’s obligation — to make payment to the holder of the cheque — is to the drawer only and that this obligation is triggered only when the cheque is presented to it.

propositions.text: Drawee must disburse funds only upon presentment by holder or holder’s agent, except as BEA provides otherwise.
propositions.quote: It is also clear that, except as provided in the BEA , the drawee is obliged, as between itself and the drawer, to disburse the funds only upon presentment of the bill by the holder — the person who is entitled to receive them — or by the holder’s agent.

paragraphs.summary: The court states drawee bank's payment duty is to drawer and triggered only by presentment by holder or agent, per BEA.

propositions.text: Delivery of cheques payable to Mr. McLeod to Trustco for deposit did not make Trustco liable to pay Mr. McLeod under s. 224(1) ITA.
propositions.quote: ... the mere fact that cheques payable to Mr. McLeod were delivered to Trustco for deposit did not make the latter liable to make a payment to the former within the meaning of s. 224(1) of the ITA .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes that delivering cheques payable to Mr. McLeod to Trustco for deposit did not make Trustco liable to pay him under s.224(1) ITA.

propositions.text: Chief Justice relies on Prof. Ogilvie's comment to support possible contract between payee and drawee bank.
propositions.quote: In her reasons in this case, the Chief Justice relies on a comment by Prof. Ogilvie in support of the proposition that there may be a contract between the payee and the drawee bank (Bank and Customer Law in Canada, at pp. 288-91).

propositions.text: Prof. Ogilvie's comment does not support broad proposition of contract between payee and drawee bank; it concerns bank's duty to present cheque timely as collecting bank.
propositions.quote: With respect, I do not read Prof. Ogilvie’s comment as supporting this broad proposition. Rather, it is in explaining the different recourses available to a bank’s customer in respect of a delayed payment ... that she states that the payee can bring an action in breach of contract against the bank ...

propositions.text: Contractual duty arises from customer's instructions as drawer or holder, not merely from payee and drawer being customers of same bank.
propositions.quote: If a bank has a contractual duty to a customer, it flows from the fact that the customer has either given the bank instructions as the drawer of the cheque and holder of the account from which the cheque is to be paid, or instructed the bank to collect the cheque as the holder of the account in which the cheque is deposited.

propositions.text: Situation differs when payee is not sole holder of account where cheque is deposited, as in this case.
propositions.quote: I would add that the situation is different where, as in the case at bar, the payee is not the sole holder of the account in which the cheque is deposited.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Prof. Ogilvie's comment does not support a contract between payee and drawee bank absent instructions; situation differs if payee is not sole account holder.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod's rights as account holder do not affect his rights as payee of cheques.
propositions.quote: In this case, Mr. McLeod’s rights as the holder of an account with the bank do not inform or affect his rights as payee of the cheques.

propositions.text: If requirements to pay did not exist and Canada made no concessions, Trustco would breach contract if it failed to pay Mr. McLeod on immediate presentment for cashing.
propositions.quote: If we assume for the sake of argument that the requirements to pay did not exist and that Canada did not make the concessions it has made, Trustco would, had Mr. McLeod presented the cheques at his branch for immediate payment to himself (i.e. cashed them), have been in breach of its contractual obligations to Mr. McLeod as the holder of the trust account had it failed to pay.

propositions.text: Cheques were deposited anonymously to joint account and had to clear before presentment for payment; deposit and presentment are distinct.
propositions.quote: Not only were the cheques deposited, anonymously, to the credit of a joint account, but they had to go through the clearance system first before being presented for payment. Capital Associates makes it clear that presentment for payment and deposit are not synonymous.

propositions.text: Distinction between deposit and presentment is critical to disposition of case.
propositions.quote: This distinction is critical to the disposition of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. McLeod's account rights don't affect payee rights; deposit and presentment differ, which is critical here.

propositions.text: Trustco received cheques for deposit and payment at different times, complicating dispute resolution.
propositions.quote: The fact that Trustco received the cheques both for deposit and for payment as drawee — although not simultaneously — has complicated the resolution of the dispute.

propositions.text: Boyd v. Emmerson involved a bank as drawee and collecting bank refusing payment due to insufficient funds after crediting cheque to customer's account.
propositions.quote: The English case of Boyd v. Emmerson (1834), 2 Ad. & E. 184, 111 E.R. 71, is one that involved facts similar to those of the instant case. ... Lord Denman C.J. held that the bank was within its right to refuse the payment, because it had taken the cheque for collection.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Trustco's dual role complicated the dispute and cites Boyd v. Emmerson where a bank refused payment after crediting cheque due to insufficient funds.

propositions.text: Boyd, Bank of Montreal, and Capital Associates show Trustco was collecting bank, not drawee, and not liable to pay Mr. McLeod.
propositions.quote: Boyd, Bank of Montreal and Capital Associates are relevant to the case at bar. ... In that capacity, it was not liable to pay any funds to Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Trustco was collecting bank, not drawee, and thus not liable to pay Mr. McLeod, citing relevant cases.

propositions.text: Being named payee on cheque does not alone make bank liable to pay that person; payment depends on drawer's instructions and endorsements.
propositions.quote: The fact that a person is designated as payee on the face of a cheque does not on its own mean that the bank is liable to make a payment to the person. ... What is on the back of the cheque — the instructions or the endorsement — is crucial to this question.

propositions.text: Here, instructions were to deposit cheques into joint account; no instructions made funds payable to Mr. McLeod personally.
propositions.quote: In this case, the instructions were to deposit the cheques into the joint account. There were no instructions that made the moneys payable to Mr. McLeod, the tax debtor.

paragraphs.summary: The court states payee designation alone doesn't impose bank liability; here, instructions directed deposit to joint account, not payment to Mr. McLeod.

propositions.text: Canada argues joint account is out of reach but treats holders as one person, Mr. McLeod, which is inconsistent.
propositions.quote: Canada cannot say that the joint account is out of reach while at the same time treating the holders of that account as one and the same person, namely Mr. McLeod.

propositions.text: Canada conceded it cannot attach funds in either account; thus Trustco's liability to pay Mr. McLeod personally cannot be confused with liability to pay joint account holders.
propositions.quote: As Canada takes the position that it could attach neither of the accounts, Trustco’s liability to pay moneys to Mr. McLeod personally cannot be confused with its liability to pay moneys to the holders of the joint account.

propositions.text: Canada had to show Trustco liable to pay Mr. McLeod or had right to attach joint account funds, which it conceded it cannot do.
propositions.quote: Canada had to show either that Trustco was liable to pay Mr. McLeod as payee, which, as I have demonstrated above, it cannot do, or that it had the right to attach the funds deposited into the joint account, which Canada has conceded it cannot do.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Canada's inconsistent position on joint account and Mr. McLeod, and that Canada conceded it cannot attach funds or show Trustco liable to pay Mr. McLeod.

propositions.text: Bank's liability to pay arises only under statute, common law, or contract; Canada relies on none here.
propositions.quote: A bank’s liability to pay can arise only under a statute, at common law or under a contract. In this case, Canada can rely on none of these sources.

propositions.text: This outcome aligns with Canada's concessions it cannot attach funds and that funds were credited to joint account, not paid to Mr. McLeod.
propositions.quote: This outcome is perfectly consistent with Canada’s concessions that it cannot attach funds in either the trust account or the joint account, and with the fact that the funds were credited by Trustco to the joint account, not paid to Mr. McLeod.

paragraphs.summary: The court states bank liability arises only under statute, common law, or contract; Canada relies on none, consistent with its concessions.

propositions.text: Accepting Canada’s position would mean payee presentment before deposit, which did not happen here.
propositions.quote: To accept Canada’s position would mean that the presentment for payment was made by the payee to the drawee before the cheques were deposited. That is not what happened in this case.

propositions.text: Accepting Trustco's liability to pay Mr. McLeod would mean drawee pays without determining cheque holder, inconsistent with law.
propositions.quote: To accept that Trustco became liable to pay Mr. McLeod would also mean that a drawee bank which honours a cheque makes payment to the payee without determining who the holder of the cheque is.

propositions.text: Canada's position conflicts with law that bank accepting cheque for deposit is not acting as drawee even if it is also drawee.
propositions.quote: Canada’s position is inconsistent with the fact that a bank that accepts a cheque for deposit does not in so doing act in the capacity of a drawee even if it also happens to be the drawee.

propositions.text: Canada's interpretation would impose undue burdens on banks to determine payee liability upon third-party demands, not required by law or BEA.
propositions.quote: Canada’s interpretation would also mean that whenever demands are made by third parties, banks would have to determine whether payees ... are liable to make payments. No such requirement exists at common law or is provided for in the BEA .

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Canada's position as inconsistent with law and impractical, noting presentment did not occur before deposit and banks are not drawees when accepting deposits.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed, prior decisions set aside, and assessments vacated with costs throughout.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I would allow the appeal, set aside the decisions of the Federal Court of Appeal and the Tax Court of Canada and vacate the assessments with costs throughout.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside prior decisions, and vacates assessments with costs.

propositions.text: The Chief Justice dissents and would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: The Chief Justice (dissenting) — Having read the reasons of Deschamps J., I am respectfully of the view that the appeal should be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Justice dissents, favoring dismissal of the appeal.

propositions.text: Two narrow points divide the court: whether bank becomes holder when cheque delivered for deposit, and whether funds in joint account are payable to both holders.
propositions.quote: While I agree with much of Deschamps J.’s analysis, there are two narrow points that divide us, and that lead us to a different result in this case.

propositions.text: Deschamps J. says bank becomes holder when cheque delivered for deposit; dissenting judge says bank collects as agent, not holder (citing B.M.P. Global).
propositions.quote: First, according to Deschamps J., when a customer delivers a cheque to his or her bank with instructions to deposit the funds into his or her account, the bank becomes the holder of the cheque, and therefore any funds collected from the cheque are paid to the bank itself. In my view, the bank does not become the holder of a cheque, but rather collects the funds as agent for its principal: B.M.P. Global Distribution Inc. v. Bank of Nova Scotia, 2009 SCC 15, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 504, at para. 83.

propositions.text: Deschamps J. argues funds in joint account are payable to both holders; dissenting judge disagrees, saying bank receives funds as payee's agent and funds are payable only to payee while in transit.
propositions.quote: Second, Deschamps J. relies on the alternative argument that where funds are deposited into a joint account, as they were here, the funds are payable to both account holders, rather than just payable to the payee of the cheque. I do not agree. In my view, a “bank receives the funds as the payee’s agent” (B.M.P., at para. 83 (emphasis added)), and while they are in transit the funds are only payable to the payee.

paragraphs.summary: The dissenting judge disagrees with Deschamps J. on whether bank becomes holder on deposit and whether joint account funds are payable to both holders.

propositions.text: Deschamps J. argues that funds in a joint account are payable to both account holders, not just the cheque payee
propositions.quote: Deschamps J. relies on the alternative argument that where funds are deposited into a joint account, as they were here, the funds are payable to both account holders, rather than just payable to the payee of the cheque.

propositions.text: I disagree and find the bank receives funds as the payee's agent, so funds in transit are payable only to the payee
propositions.quote: In my view, a “bank receives the funds as the payee’s agent” (B.M.P., at para. 83 (emphasis added)), and while they are in transit the funds are only payable to the payee.

propositions.text: I will develop these points below
propositions.quote: I develop these points below.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker argues joint account funds are payable to both holders; the Court disagrees, finding funds in transit payable only to the payee and will explain further.

propositions.text: Bank concedes the only live question is whether it was liable to pay Mr. McLeod as a result of the cheques he wrote to himself.
propositions.quote: In this appeal, Canada Trustco Mortgage Company (the “Bank”) concedes that the only live question is whether it was liable to make a payment to the tax debtor (“Mr. McLeod”) as a result of the cheques he wrote to himself.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent notes the bank concedes the only issue is its liability to pay Mr. McLeod for the cheques he wrote to himself.

propositions.text: The case concerns a tax debtor drawing a cheque to himself, with drawee and collecting bank being the same institution.
propositions.quote: It is central to the analysis that we are dealing exclusively with the circumstances in which a tax debtor draws a cheque in favour of him- or herself, and not a third party. It is also important to bear in mind that, in this case, the drawee bank is the same as the collecting bank.

paragraphs.summary: The dissent emphasizes the case involves a tax debtor drawing a cheque to himself and the drawee and collecting bank are the same.

propositions.text: I will review legal principles and explain application of s. 224(1) of the Income Tax Act to these facts.
propositions.quote: I will first briefly review the applicable legal principles. I will then go on to explain the application of s. 224(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp .) (“ITA ”), to the facts before us.

paragraphs.summary: The Court will review legal principles and explain application of s. 224(1) of the Income Tax Act to the facts.

propositions.text: Section 224(1) allows Minister to require payment to Receiver General of monies payable to tax debtor.
propositions.quote: 224. (1) Where . . . a person is . . . liable to make a payment to another person . . . (. . . the “tax debtor”), the Minister may . . . require the person to pay . . . the moneys otherwise payable to the tax debtor . . . to the Receiver General on account of the tax debtor’s liability . . . .

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 224(1) allows Minister to require payment to Receiver General of monies payable to tax debtor.

propositions.text: 'Liable' means responsible at law, not limited to debtor-creditor relationship.
propositions.quote: The ordinary meaning of the word “liable” in a legal context is to denote the fact that a person is responsible at law.

propositions.text: Section 224(1) extends beyond debtor-creditor relationships to any case where trustee is liable to pay taxpayer.
propositions.quote: the demand on third parties [a subsection 224(1) requirement] by which the Crown’s claim is made in this case is not confined to a debtor-creditor relationship, as is a garnishee order; it is stated to extend to any case where the trustee is “liable to make a payment to the taxpayer”.

propositions.text: Tax Court Judge erred by limiting 'liable to make a payment' to debtor-creditor relationships only.
propositions.quote: It is my respectful view, therefore, that the Tax Court Judge was wrong in law to limit the phrase “liable to make a payment” only to situations where a debtor-creditor relationship exists.

propositions.text: The relevant question is whether respondent had legal responsibility to pay tax debtor on 1 February 1994.
propositions.quote: It is this: did the respondent have a responsibility at law to make a payment to the tax debtor on 1 February 1994?

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains 'liable' means legal responsibility beyond debtor-creditor, finds Tax Court erred limiting it, and poses relevant question on legal responsibility.

propositions.text: 'Payable' is not a term of art and should be interpreted by ordinary dictionary meaning.
propositions.quote: The word “payable” is not a term of art. Nor is it defined in the regulations. I do not see that it was used in any special sense.

propositions.text: 'Payable' means when claimant is entitled by contract or law to enforce payment.
propositions.quote: the word “payable” in s. 58(8)(b)(i) [of the Unemployment Insurance Act] refers to the point in time when vacation pay is due to a claimant in the sense that he is entitled by his contract of employment or by the general law to have it paid to him and his employer is under an obligation to pay it.

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authorities that 'payable' means when payment is legally enforceable, not a technical term.

propositions.text: Person served with requirement to pay must have legal responsibility to pay tax debtor.
propositions.quote: the person or institution served by the Minister with a requirement to pay must have a responsibility at law to make a payment to the tax debtor.

propositions.text: Section 224(1) applies broadly where tax debtor can enforce payment from party served.
propositions.quote: The scope of the operation of s. 224(1) is not narrowly confined, but exists wherever the tax debtor is in a position at law to enforce payment from the party served with the requirement to pay.

propositions.text: A restrictive view would undermine the Minister's power under s. 224(1).
propositions.quote: To adopt a more restrictive view of its content would be to undermine the proper functioning of the power the provision grants the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 224(1) applies broadly where tax debtor can enforce payment; restrictive views undermine Minister's power.

propositions.text: I now consider the legal relationship between bank and customer under s. 224(1).
propositions.quote: With this understanding of the governing provision in mind, I turn now to the nature of the legal relationship between the bank and its customer and how it plays out within the parameters of s. 224(1) .

paragraphs.summary: The Court will now analyze the bank-customer legal relationship under s. 224(1).

propositions.text: Bank-customer relationship is debtor-creditor; bank is debtor, duty triggered by customer's demand.
propositions.quote: The relationship between a bank and its customer is one of creditor and debtor, where the bank is the debtor: Foley v. Hill (1848), 2 H.L.C. 28, 9 E.R. 1002. The duty of repayment is triggered when the customer makes a demand for payment from the bank.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states bank-customer relationship is debtor-creditor; bank owes repayment duty upon customer's demand.

propositions.text: Drawee bank owes legal obligations only to drawer, not payee; no privity with payee.
propositions.quote: Ordinarily, the bank on which a cheque is drawn (the drawee bank) is under no liability to pay the payee of a cheque; its legal obligations are owed exclusively to its customer (the drawer)

propositions.text: This principle confirmed by Bills of Exchange Act ss. 16(1) and 126.
propositions.quote: This principle is confirmed by ss. 16(1) and 126 of the Bills of Exchange Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. B-4 (“BEA ”).

propositions.text: Legal relationship between drawer and drawee bank arises from banking contract; payee not party to contract.
propositions.quote: The legal relationship between the drawer and the drawee bank arises from the banking contract between them; if the payee is not a party to this contract, it is not in privity with the bank.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains drawee bank owes obligations only to drawer under contract; payee has no privity with bank.

propositions.text: If payee and drawer are same person, bank is liable to payee once cheque presented.
propositions.quote: where the payee and the drawer are the same person, i.e. when an individual writes a cheque to him- or herself, the bank is liable to the payee once the cheque is presented.

propositions.text: Bank has contractual duty to pay customer when cheque to self is presented and properly payable.
propositions.quote: the bank is under a contractual duty to pay the cheque once it is presented and once it has ensured that it is properly payable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states bank is liable to payee if payee and drawer are same person, with contractual duty to pay cheque.

propositions.text: If payee and drawer are customers of same bank, payee can sue bank directly for breach of contract.
propositions.quote: where the drawer and payee are customers of the same bank, the payee can sue directly in breach of contract, as well for a delay in collection

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes payee can sue bank directly if payee and drawer are customers of same bank.

propositions.text: Bank argues deposited cheques become payable to bank under BEA s. 165(3), not to payee.
propositions.quote: once the cheques were deposited, they were no longer “payable” to Mr. McLeod, but “were now payable to the Bank pursuant to subsection 165(3) of the Bills of Exchange Act ”

propositions.text: Bank says payment on deposited cheque is made to bank alone, so s. 224(1) cannot be triggered.
propositions.quote: once a cheque is delivered to a bank for collection, the bank becomes the holder of the cheque, and any payment made on the cheque is made to the bank alone. Consequently, s. 224(1) of the ITA cannot be triggered

propositions.text: Deschamps J. accepted Bank's proposition that deposited cheques are payable to bank, not payee.
propositions.quote: The reasons of Deschamps J. accept this proposition.

propositions.text: I cannot accept Bank's proposition that deposited cheques are payable to bank, not payee.
propositions.quote: With respect, I cannot.

paragraphs.summary: The Bank and Deschamps J. argue deposited cheques are payable to bank, not payee; the Court rejects this.

propositions.text: Bank misstates relationship; bank collects funds as agent for customer (payee).
propositions.quote: a bank that collects the funds from a deposited cheque receives the funds as agent for the customer (the payee)

propositions.text: B.M.P. and Westminster Bank confirm bank acts as agent for payee when collecting cheque funds.
propositions.quote: B.M.P.; see also Westminster Bank Ltd. v. Hilton (1926), 43 T.L.R. 124 (H.L.), at p. 126.

propositions.text: Two transactions occur: funds credited to payee, then received back by bank under contract.
propositions.quote: This involves two transactions. The funds are initially “credit[ed] . . . to its principal”, the payee/customer: B.M.P., at para. 77, per Deschamps J. The bank then “receive[s] them back under the banking contract” (ibid.).

propositions.text: These are distinct episodes; deposited cheque is payable to customer, never to bank.
propositions.quote: The fact that these transactions follow one on the other does not change the conclusion that, legally, they are two distinct episodes. As such, a deposited cheque is payable to the customer when it is deposited; at no time is the cheque payable to the bank.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds bank collects cheque funds as agent for payee; deposited cheque payable to customer, not bank.

propositions.text: Clearing system is neutral; it should not break chain of possession of funds.
propositions.quote: this Court argued against employing a formalistic analysis to describe transactions through the clearing system, stating that the clearing system should be a neutral factor

propositions.text: Funds remain traceable after clearing; bank handles funds as agent for customer.
propositions.quote: I prefer to assess the traceability of the asset after the clearing process and not see that process as a systematic break in the chain of possession of the funds. Just as the collecting bank receives the funds as the payee’s agent, the clearing system is only a payment process.

propositions.text: When customer deposits cheque to self, clearing process does not affect bank's agency role.
propositions.quote: Where a customer draws a cheque in favour of him- or herself and deposits that cheque into another account, we should attach no significance to the fact that the moneys pass through a clearing process and the fact that a bank handles the funds as agent for its customer.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds clearing system is neutral; funds remain traceable; bank acts as agent despite clearing process.

propositions.text: BEA s. 165(3) does not make bank a holder of the cheque.
propositions.quote: s. 165(3) of the BEA does not establish that the bank becomes a holder of the cheque.

propositions.text: BEA s. 165(3) states bank acquiring rights and powers of holder in due course when crediting cheque deposit.
propositions.quote: Where a cheque is delivered to a bank for deposit to the credit of a person and the bank credits him with the amount of the cheque, the bank acquires all the rights and powers of a holder in due course of the cheque.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds BEA s. 165(3) grants bank rights of holder in due course but does not make bank holder of cheque.

propositions.text: Distinction exists between actual holder payable cheque and acquiring rights of holder in due course.
propositions.quote: There is an important distinction between an actual holder of a cheque to whom the cheque is payable, and merely acquiring “all the rights and powers of a holder in due course”.

propositions.text: Boma Manufacturing and Crawford explain s. 165(3) protects collecting bank from liability for fraudulent cheques.
propositions.quote: The narrow object of s. 165(3) was described by Iacobucci J. in Boma as follows: When a collecting bank is presented with a cheque for deposit to the credit of the payee, the bank is entitled, essentially, to assume that it was truly the intention of the drawer that the payee receive the proceeds of the cheque.

paragraphs.summary: The Court distinguishes actual cheque holder from rights of holder in due course; s. 165(3) protects collecting bank from liability.

propositions.text: s. 165(3) aims to protect collecting bank from liability for fraudulent cheques, not to make bank holder.
propositions.quote: Subsection 165(3) sought to clear the collecting bank from liability when it deposits fraudulent cheques. This limited objective is achieved by granting the collecting bank “all the rights and powers of a holder in due course”, and does not require the bank to be actually designated a holder in due course

propositions.text: Bank's use of s. 165(3) to claim cheque payable to bank is unrelated to provision's purpose and rejected.
propositions.quote: I agree with the respondent that the Bank’s use of this provision bears no relation to its purpose and should be rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 165(3) protects bank from liability but does not make bank holder; rejects Bank's contrary use.

propositions.text: Deposited cheque is payable to payee, never to bank except as agent for payee.
propositions.quote: I conclude that a deposited cheque is payable to the payee, and at no time is it payable to the bank other than as agent for the payee.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes deposited cheque is payable to payee, not bank except as agent.

propositions.text: Deschamps J. reasoned bank liable only to joint account holders jointly if not cheque holder.
propositions.quote: The reasons of Justice Deschamps further argue that if the Bank was not itself the holder of the cheque, then the Bank was only ever liable to the two account holders jointly.

propositions.text: Court finds majority's result wrong in law and unfortunate in impact.
propositions.quote: With respect, it seems to me that the result of the majority is wrong in law and unfortunate in its impact.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Deschamps J.'s reasoning on bank liability to joint account holders wrong in law and unfortunate.

propositions.text: Minister cannot garnish funds once in joint account but can intercept funds in transit before deposit.
propositions.quote: I agree that the Minister could not garnish moneys once they were in the joint account. However, it does not follow that the Minister could not intercept funds in transit before they arrived in the joint account.

propositions.text: Section 224(1) intercepts funds while in transit.
propositions.quote: A requirement to pay in s. 224(1) of the ITA intercepts funds while they are in transit.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Minister cannot garnish joint account funds but can intercept funds in transit under s. 224(1).

propositions.text: Funds in joint account become joint property and cannot be garnished individually.
propositions.quote: Once funds are irrevocably deposited in a joint account, they become the property of joint account holders jointly under the terms of their banking contract.

propositions.text: Joint account funds cannot be garnished by Minister if only one account holder owes debt.
propositions.quote: Since neither joint account holder could sue the bank on his or her own for recovery of the funds, it follows that the account cannot be garnished when only one of the two account holders owes a debt to a third party.

propositions.text: Rationale: joint account holders must sue jointly; individual garnishment not allowed.
propositions.quote: Since all monies deposited in a joint account are deemed to be joint property, neither joint account holder individually may sue the bank for recovery of funds in the account. Such an action is one in debt . . . and the joint creditors of the bank, the joint account holders, must sue jointly.

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites authorities that joint account funds are joint property and cannot be garnished individually.

propositions.text: Before funds arrive in a joint account, the drawee bank is liable only to the payee of the cheque.
propositions.quote: before the funds arrive in the joint account and while the funds are being transferred, the drawee bank is only liable to make a payment to the payee of the cheque.

propositions.text: The other joint account holder has no right to funds before they arrive in the account.
propositions.quote: The other joint account holder had no right to the funds before they arrived in the account.

propositions.text: Mr. McLeod could have sued the Bank if it failed to honour his cheque.
propositions.quote: Mr. McLeod could have sued the Bank on his own if the Bank failed to honour his cheque.

propositions.text: Only the tax debtor’s status as payee matters to trigger s. 224(1) with a joint account.
propositions.quote: it is only the tax debtor’s status as payee that matters for the purpose of triggering s. 224(1) , in the presence of a joint account.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that before funds reach a joint account, only the payee is entitled and only their status triggers s. 224(1).

propositions.text: When a requirement to pay is issued, the Minister must identify the tax debtor involved.
propositions.quote: when a requirement to pay is issued, the Minister must indicate the identity of the tax debtor involved.

propositions.text: Banks are only required to redirect payments to tax debtors named by the Minister, not monitor unknown third parties' liabilities.
propositions.quote: Banks issued with a requirement to pay are thus never put in the position of having to monitor the liabilities of unknown third parties: they are only required to redirect payments that they are liable to make to tax debtors specifically named by the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Minister must name the tax debtor, so banks only redirect payments to known debtors, not monitor others.

propositions.text: Deschamps J.'s view on joint accounts may negatively affect other law areas, like family maintenance.
propositions.quote: Deschamps J.’s view of the legal significance of the joint account in this case may negatively impact other areas of the law.

propositions.text: Restrictive interpretation of garnishment powers could defeat child and spousal support due to joint accounts.
propositions.quote: There are potentially dangerous repercussions of a restrictive interpretation of garnishment powers when applied, for example, to family maintenance. Child and spousal support ought not be defeated by the mere existence of a joint account.

paragraphs.summary: The court warns that a narrow view of joint accounts could harm family maintenance law and support enforcement.

propositions.text: Once the Bank received Mr. McLeod’s cheques, its liability to him was triggered and it was contractually bound to pay.
propositions.quote: once the Bank received Mr. McLeod’s cheques to himself, its liability to its customer was triggered. The Bank was therefore contractually bound to honour its customer’s demand to pay him.

propositions.text: All s. 224(1) requirements were met and the requirement to pay attached to money in transit between Mr. McLeod’s accounts.
propositions.quote: all of the requirements of s. 224(1) were met, and the requirement to pay attached to the money in transit between Mr. McLeod’s accounts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Bank's liability was triggered and s. 224(1) requirements met for money in transit between Mr. McLeod’s accounts.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs; McLachlin C.J. and Fish and Abella JJ. dissent.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs. Appeal allowed with costs, McLachlin C.J. and Fish and Abella JJ. dissenting.

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellant and respondent are named.
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellant: McCarthy Tétrault, Toronto. Solicitor for the respondent: Attorney General of Canada, Ottawa.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs, noting dissenting judges and naming solicitors for parties.
